items.authorNote: M1 sample drafted by Claude Code, 2026-10-09; format and content reviewed by Steve Grant, 2026-10-10. Unpublished until the habit's full set is written (M2). Exemplars must be plausible: the flawed one should be something a capable beginning teacher would write.
items.title: A puck on ice
items.moment: The start of a lesson on balanced and unbalanced forces, before students try prediction questions on their own.
items.studentProfile: Year 7. Many believe a moving object needs a force to keep it moving, and that it slows down when the force ‘runs out’. They can draw simple force arrows.
items.task: Write what you’ll say as you model your thinking on this question — A puck slides across smooth ice after the player stops pushing it. What happens to its speed, and why? — and what students will do straight afterwards.
selfCheck: You narrate at least one decision, not just the answer.
You voice the tempting wrong idea and show how you check it.
Your commentary is short enough for Year 7s to follow.
Students do some of the thinking aloud straight afterwards.

exemplars.text: “I want to say it slows down because my push has run out. That’s my gut — let me check it. What forces are acting on the puck now, after the push? Gravity down, the ice pushing up. Friction? On smooth ice, almost none. So the forces are very nearly balanced, and balanced forces mean no change in motion. It keeps going at almost the same speed — only that tiny bit of friction slows it. My gut was wrong, and that question is how I caught it.” Then students get the same question about a trolley on a smooth bench and talk it through with a partner, starting with ‘What forces are acting now?’ while I listen.

annotations.quote: That’s my gut — let me check it.
annotations.comment: Voices the misconception students actually hold as a tempting first thought, then marks the moment of checking.

annotations.quote: What forces are acting on the puck now, after the push?
annotations.comment: A checking question students can reuse on any motion problem.

annotations.quote: starting with ‘What forces are acting now?’ while I listen
annotations.comment: Hands over straight away, with the same question as the prompt, and the teacher listening in.

exemplars.summary: Voices the tempting idea, checks it with a reusable question, and hands over at once.

exemplars.text: “Let’s think about this carefully. The puck is sliding on ice. What forces act on it? Gravity pulls it down, the ice pushes it up, and there’s almost no friction. So the forces are nearly balanced, and the speed stays almost the same. That’s Newton’s first law.” Then students answer five similar questions in their books.

annotations.comment: A good checking question, clearly modelled.

annotations.quote: So the forces are nearly balanced, and the speed stays almost the same.
annotations.comment: Fluent and correct, but there’s no stuck point. The idea students actually hold is never voiced, so they never see it being caught.

annotations.quote: Then students answer five similar questions in their books.
annotations.comment: No handover: students practise producing answers, not the thinking they watched.

exemplars.summary: Clear and accurate, and it models a useful question — but it’s a performance with no stuck point, and no handover.

exemplars.text: “Newton’s first law says an object keeps moving at a constant speed unless an unbalanced force acts on it. Ice has very little friction, so the puck keeps going. Write that down: no unbalanced force, no change in speed.” Then students copy the law and its definition.

annotations.comment: Starts from the answer, so there’s no thinking left to model. This is explaining, not modelling.
The product is the focus. Students copy; they don’t decide or check anything.

exemplars.summary: Correct physics, taught as a statement to copy. Useful at another moment, but it isn’t modelling thinking.

items.title: Reading a pedigree
items.moment: The first lesson on pedigrees. Students have just learned to complete Punnett squares.
items.studentProfile: Year 10. Confident with Punnett squares, but when reading a pedigree they guess the pattern of inheritance from how often the trait appears, rather than reasoning from who is affected.
items.task: Write what you’ll say as you model your thinking on a pedigree where two unaffected parents have an affected daughter — is the trait dominant or recessive, and is it autosomal or X-linked? — and what students will do straight afterwards.
selfCheck: You narrate at least one decision, not just the conclusion.
You voice a tempting wrong idea and show how you check it.
Your commentary is short enough to follow on first hearing.
Students think aloud on a pedigree of their own straight afterwards.

exemplars.text: “Two unaffected parents, affected daughter. My first instinct is to count how many people have it — but that won’t tell me the pattern. Better question: could it be dominant? If it were, at least one parent would have to show it. Neither does, so it’s recessive. Next: could it be on the X? A daughter with an X-linked recessive trait needs an affected father, and he isn’t affected. So it’s autosomal recessive.” Then pairs take the next pedigree, one partner thinking aloud with two questions on the board — ‘Could it be dominant?’ and ‘Could it be on the X?’ — while I listen in.

annotations.quote: My first instinct is to count how many people have it
annotations.comment: Voices the guessing habit these students actually have, then replaces it.

annotations.quote: Could it be on the X?
annotations.comment: Each step is a question students can reuse on any pedigree.

annotations.quote: one partner thinking aloud with two questions on the board
annotations.comment: Hands over at once, with the same questions as prompts.

exemplars.summary: Provisional (Steve to write). One pedigree, a voiced wrong instinct, reusable questions, and an immediate handover.

exemplars.text: “I’ll think out loud. Two unaffected parents, affected daughter. My first thought is dominant, because it’s showing up — hang on, if it were dominant, one parent would have to show it. Neither does, so it’s recessive. Is it on the X? If it were X-linked recessive, the daughter would need an affected father, and he isn’t. So it’s autosomal recessive.” I then talk through the next two pedigrees the same way, a few minutes each, before students do the worksheet’s remaining pedigrees on their own.

annotations.quote: My first thought is dominant, because it’s showing up — hang on
annotations.comment: A genuine stuck point, with a tempting idea voiced and caught: the strongest part.

annotations.quote: If it were X-linked recessive, the daughter would need an affected father
annotations.comment: Reasoning students can borrow, framed as a check.

annotations.quote: I then talk through the next two pedigrees the same way
annotations.comment: Three think-alouds in a row: the monologue. By the third, students are copying conclusions rather than following decisions.

annotations.quote: before students do the worksheet’s remaining pedigrees on their own
annotations.comment: Silent, individual practice: students never think aloud themselves.

exemplars.summary: The first pedigree is modelled well. Then it becomes a monologue, and there’s no handover.

exemplars.text: “Here are the rules for pedigrees. If two unaffected parents have an affected child, the trait is recessive. If an affected daughter has an unaffected father, the trait isn’t X-linked recessive. Copy these rules into your books, then use them on the worksheet.”

annotations.quote: Here are the rules for pedigrees.
annotations.comment: Starts from conclusions. There’s no thinking left to model.

annotations.quote: Copy these rules into your books
annotations.comment: Students apply rules they haven’t reasoned through, so they can’t adapt when a pedigree doesn’t fit.

exemplars.summary: Provisional. Accurate rules, taught to be copied: explaining, not modelling thinking.
